title: Breadth-first search (BFS), levels and paths
overview: BFS explores a graph layer by layer from a source using a queue. Because it reaches nodes in order of distance, the same code also gives the shortest number of edges to every node (its level) and, with a parent array, the actual shortest path. These patterns come back in almost every later graph problem.

concepts.explain: Push the source, mark it visited. Repeatedly pop the front node and push every unvisited neighbour, marking it visited **when it is pushed** so it never enters the queue twice.
Set `level[src] = 0` and `level[child] = level[par] + 1`. In an unweighted graph this is the fewest edges from the source.
Store `parent[child] = par` when a child is discovered. Walking `parent` back from the destination gives the path in reverse.
After one BFS, `vis[x]` tells whether `x` can be reached from the source at all.
`memset(vis, false, ...)` and `memset(level, -1, ...)` before each BFS; `-1` means "not reached". `memset` needs `<cstring>`.
Every node is pushed once and every edge is looked at once (twice when undirected): O(V + E).

files.title: BFS traversal
files.what: Builds an undirected graph and prints the nodes in the order BFS visits them from node 0.
steps: Read the edges into `adj_list` (both directions).
Clear `visited` with `memset`, then call `bfs(0)`.
In `bfs`, push `src` and mark it visited.
Pop the front node `par`, print it, and push each unvisited `child`, marking it right away.
The loop ends when the queue is empty: every reachable node was printed once.
files.input_note: `n e`, then `e` edges. BFS always starts from node 0.
files.output_note: `0 1 2 3 4 5`: first 0, then its neighbours 1 and 2, then their neighbours 3 and 4, then 5.
files.watch_out: Tip: on some compilers you need `#include <cstring>` for `memset`; this file relies on another header bringing it in.

check.q: Why mark a node visited when it is pushed instead of when it is popped?
check.a: Otherwise the same node could be pushed several times by different parents before it is popped.

files.title: Shortest distance with BFS levels
files.what: Adds a `level` array to BFS so that after one run it knows the distance (in edges) from the source to every node.
steps: Read the graph, then `src` and `dest`.
Set all `level` to `-1` (unreached) and `level[src] = 0`.
When a child is discovered: `level[child] = level[par] + 1`.
BFS still prints its visiting order, then the program prints `level of dest`.
files.input_note: `n e`, the edges, then one line `src dest`.
files.output_note: `0 1 2 3 4 5 level of 5 = 3`: the BFS order, then the answer 3 (path 0-1-3-5).
files.watch_out: Tip: on some compilers you need `#include <cstring>` for `memset`; this file relies on another header bringing it in.

check.q: What does `level[x] == -1` mean after the BFS?
check.a: Node `x` cannot be reached from the source.

files.title: Can we reach a node?
files.what: Runs BFS from `src` and answers YES if `dest` got visited.
steps: Build the graph, read `src` and `dest`.
Run `bfs(src)`; it marks every reachable node in `visited`.
If `visited[dest]` is true print YES, otherwise NO.
files.input_note: `n e`, edges, then `src dest`. Here 0 and 2 are in the same piece; 4-5 is a separate piece.
files.output_note: `0 1 3 2 YES << endl`: the BFS order and then the answer (with a stray ` << endl` in the text, see Watch out).
files.watch_out: The quotes are misplaced: `cout << "YES << endl";` prints the text ` << endl` literally. Write `cout << "YES" << endl;`. Tip: on some compilers you need `#include <cstring>` for `memset`; this file relies on another header bringing it in.

check.q: After a BFS from `s`, how do you test if `t` is reachable in O(1)?

files.title: Print the shortest path
files.what: Records each node's `parent` during BFS, then walks back from the destination to print the path, first reversed and then in the right order.
steps: Set `parent` to `-1` for all nodes (the source keeps -1).
When a child is discovered: `parent[child] = par`.
Way 1: start at `dest`, print `node`, move to `parent[node]` until you hit -1. This is dest → src.
Way 2: collect the same nodes in a vector `path`, `reverse` it, then print src → dest.
files.output_note: Everything on one line: `0 1 2 3 4 5` (BFS order), `5 3 1 0` (reversed path), `0 1 3 5` (correct path).
files.watch_out: The three prints have no line breaks between them, so add `cout << endl;` to read them easily. Tip: on some compilers you need `#include <cstring>` for `memset`; this file relies on another header bringing it in.

check.q: Why does the backward walk stop?
check.a: The source's parent is -1, and the loop runs while `node != -1`.

files.title: Many shortest-distance queries
files.what: For each query `(S, D)` it runs a fresh BFS from S and prints the level of D (or -1).
steps: Build the graph once.
For each query, `bfs(src)` first resets `visited` and `level` itself.
After the BFS, `level[dest]` is the answer (-1 if unreachable).
files.input_note: `n e`, edges, `Q`, then Q lines `S D`.
files.output_note: Each line starts with the BFS order (a leftover debug print) and ends with the answer: `level of 5 = 2`, `level of 5 = 3`, `level of 0 = 0`. The judge expects only `2`, `3`, `0`.
files.watch_out: For the judge, remove the `cout << par` debug line and print only `level[dest]`. Tip: on some compilers you need `#include <cstring>` for `memset`; this file relies on another header bringing it in.

check.q: Why must `visited` and `level` be reset for every query?
check.a: Each query uses a different source; old marks would stop the new BFS from visiting nodes.

files.title: Nodes at level L
files.what: BFS from node 0 and collects every node whose level equals L, then prints them in descending order.
steps: Run BFS from 0 while computing `level`.
When a node is popped, if `level[par] == l` push it into `nodes`.
Sort `nodes` with `greater<int>()` and print.
files.complexity: Time O(V + E + k log k) · Space O(V)
files.output_note: `L = 1` prints `3 2 1`: the three neighbours of 0, largest first.
files.watch_out: Tip: on some compilers you need `#include <cstring>` for `memset`; this file relies on another header bringing it in.

check.q: How do you sort a vector in descending order?

files.title: Count direct neighbours
files.what: No search needed: the number of nodes directly connected to N is the size of its adjacency list.
steps: Build the adjacency list.
Read `node`.
Print `adj_list[node].size()`.
files.complexity: Time O(V + E) to build, O(1) per answer
files.output_note: The output `3` means node 1 touches three nodes (0, 2 and 3).

check.q: What is `adj_list[x].size()` called in graph language?

files.title: LeetCode 841 - Keys and Rooms
files.what: Rooms are nodes and keys are directed edges. BFS from room 0; if every room gets visited, the answer is true.
steps: `rooms[i]` is already an adjacency list: the keys found in room i.
`bfs(0, rooms)` visits every room we can unlock.
Loop over all rooms; if any `vis[i]` is false, return false.
Otherwise return true.
files.complexity: Time O(n + total keys) · Space O(n)
files.input_note: Test driver format: number of cases; for each: `n`, then n lines `k key1 .. keyk`. These are LeetCode's two examples.
files.output_note: `true` then `false`, which match LeetCode's expected answers (in example 2, room 2's only key is locked inside room 2).

check.q: Why is this a graph problem even though the word graph never appears?
check.a: Rooms are nodes and a key in room a for room b is an edge a → b; the question is whether all nodes are reachable from 0.

files.title: CSES Message Route (BFS plus a parent array)
files.what: Send a message from computer 1 to computer n through as few computers as possible. Print how many computers the route uses and the route itself, or IMPOSSIBLE. Every connection costs the same, so the shortest route is the one with fewest edges, and that is exactly a BFS level.
steps: Read the graph into `vector<vector<int>> adj_list(n + 1)` and push both directions, because a connection works both ways. A vector, not a fixed `adj_list[1005]`: here n can be in the hundreds of thousands.
BFS from computer 1, filling `level` and `parent` as each computer is discovered.
`parent[child] = par` records who put the child into the queue, so the route can be walked backwards later.
If computer n was never visited, print IMPOSSIBLE and stop.
Otherwise start at n and follow `parent` until it is -1. Computer 1 keeps parent -1, so that is what ends the walk.
The collected route comes out from n back to 1, so `reverse` it before printing.
Print `path.size()` first (the number of computers, one more than `level[n]`), then the route on the next line.
files.complexity: Time O(n + m) · Space O(n + m)
files.input_note: `n m`, then m lines `a b`. Computers are numbered from 1. This is the problem's own sample: 5 computers and 5 connections.
files.output_note: Prints `3` and then `1 4 5`. The message goes 1 -> 4 -> 5, three computers in total. With the second sample in the file header (`4 2`, edges 1-2 and 3-4) it prints `IMPOSSIBLE`, because nothing joins the two halves.
files.watch_out: The count asked for is computers, not connections: it is `level[n] + 1`, not `level[n]`. And check `visited[n]` before touching the parents - walking back from a computer that was never reached gives nonsense.

check.q: Why is plain BFS enough here, without any distances?
check.a: Every connection counts the same, so the cheapest route is simply the one with the fewest connections, and BFS reaches every computer on its lowest level first.

recap: BFS = queue + visited; mark when you push.
`level[child] = level[par] + 1` gives shortest distance in unweighted graphs.
`parent[child] = par` lets you rebuild the path; reverse it at the end.

check_yourself.q: Why does BFS give shortest distances only when all edges have the same weight?
check_yourself.a: It counts edges layer by layer; with different weights a path with more edges can be cheaper.

check_yourself.q: A BFS from node 0 never reaches node 7. What are `level[7]` and `parent[7]`?
check_yourself.a: Both stay at their start value, -1.

check_yourself.q: What data structure turns BFS into DFS if you swap it in?
check_yourself.a: A stack (LIFO) instead of a queue (FIFO).

body: You are standing in town 0 and you want to reach town 5 using as few roads as possible. Here is the map:

Left to yourself you would not wander around. You would write down every town one road away: 1 and 2. Then every new town two roads away: 3 and 4. Then three roads away: 5. The moment 5 appears you stop, and you know the answer is 3 roads, because you had already finished with everything closer.

That ring-by-ring sweep is **breadth-first search**, and you have done it before. In the binary tree module, level order printed the root, then the whole first level, then the whole second level, using a queue: pop a node, push its children. BFS is that same loop with `adj_list[par]` in place of `left` and `right`.

**What is new is one array.** A tree has no way back to a node you already printed, so nothing could repeat. A graph does have a way back: standing on 1, one of its neighbours is 0, the town you came from. Push it again and 0 pushes 1 again, and the queue never empties. So every node gets marked in a `visited` array, and only unmarked neighbours are pushed.
Mark the node when you **push** it, not when you pop it. If you waited until the pop, node 5 would be pushed once by 3 and again by 4 before either push was noticed, and it would be handled twice.
Run the loop on the map above, starting at 0, and keep a `level` next to each node, `level[child] = level[par] + 1`:
intro.trace:
pop   queue after   newly pushed   level set
 -     0             0              0 -> 0
 0     1 2           1, 2           1 -> 1, 2 -> 1
 1     2 3           3              3 -> 2
 2     3 4           4              4 -> 2
 3     4 5           5              5 -> 3
 4     5             -
 5     (empty)       -

body: Read the last column: `level[5]` is 3, which is the answer you worked out by hand. And you did not only solve it for 5. One run of BFS filled in the distance to **every** town the source can reach, in O(V + E), because each node enters the queue once and each edge is looked at once.

Why is that level really the shortest distance? Because the queue keeps the towns in the order they were found, so everything at distance 1 leaves the queue before anything at distance 2. The first time a node is reached, it is reached by the fewest edges, and after that it is marked and never reconsidered.

That argument leans on one quiet assumption: **every edge counts the same, one step**. If one road took five minutes and another took two hours, a path with more roads could be quicker, and counting edges would give the wrong answer. Weighted graphs need a different algorithm, which comes later in the course.

Two small additions make BFS answer two more questions. **Which towns can I reach at all?** After the run, `visited[x]` already says so, and a node in a separate piece of the graph keeps its `level` of -1.

**Which roads do I actually take?** Store `parent[child] = par` at the moment the child is discovered, then walk backwards from the destination. On the trace above: 5 came from 3, 3 came from 1, 1 came from 0, and 0's parent is -1, so the walk stops. That gives `5 3 1 0`; reverse it and you have the path `0 1 3 5`.

The programs below are these pieces one at a time: plain BFS, BFS with levels, a reachability check, path printing, and three practice problems that reuse them. Watch the resetting: every new BFS from a new source must clear `visited` and `level` first, or the old marks will stop it.

walkthrough.heading: Watch it happen: one BFS from town 0
body: This is the map from the top of the page, swept ring by ring. Watch two things only: which towns have turned into `[x]` (marked visited), and which cell of the `level` row gets filled in. Nothing is ever filled in twice.
walkthrough.frames_title: Press the arrows to step through the queue

frames.label: Push the source into the queue, mark it visited at once, and write `level[0] = 0` because 0 is zero roads from itself.
frames.art:
(1)---(3)
  /         \
[0]         (5)
  \         /
   (2)---(4)
[x] = visited, (x) = not yet

queue:  0            just popped: -
node    0  1  2  3  4  5
level   0  -  -  -  -  -
        ^ set to 0

frames.label: Pop 0. Its neighbours 1 and 2 are both unmarked, so each one is pushed and marked in the same breath, at `level[0] + 1 = 1`.
frames.art:
[1]---(3)
  /         \
[0]         (5)
  \         /
   [2]---(4)
[x] = visited, (x) = not yet

queue:  1 2          just popped: 0
node    0  1  2  3  4  5
level   0  1  1  -  -  -
           ^  ^ set to level[0] + 1

frames.label: Pop 1. One of its neighbours is 0, the town we came from, but 0 is already marked so it is skipped - that skip is what stops the queue going round for ever. Town 3 is new, so it joins the back at level 2.
frames.art:
[1]---[3]
  /         \
[0]         (5)
  \         /
   [2]---(4)
[x] = visited, (x) = not yet

queue:  2 3          just popped: 1
node    0  1  2  3  4  5
level   0  1  1  2  -  -
                 ^ set to level[1] + 1

frames.label: Pop 2. Same story along the bottom road: 0 is skipped, 4 is new and lands at level 2. Both towns two roads away are now found, and neither was found early.
frames.art:
[1]---[3]
  /         \
[0]         (5)
  \         /
   [2]---[4]
[x] = visited, (x) = not yet

queue:  3 4          just popped: 2
node    0  1  2  3  4  5
level   0  1  1  2  2  -
                    ^ set to level[2] + 1

frames.label: Pop 3. Town 5 is reached for the very first time, from 3, so `level[5] = 2 + 1 = 3`. This is the moment the answer is written down.
frames.art:
[1]---[3]
  /         \
[0]         [5]
  \         /
   [2]---[4]
[x] = visited, (x) = not yet

queue:  4 5          just popped: 3
node    0  1  2  3  4  5
level   0  1  1  2  2  3
                       ^ set to level[3] + 1

frames.label: Pop 4. Its neighbours are 2 and 5, and both are already marked, so nothing is pushed. Had we marked on the pop instead of the push, 4 would have queued 5 a second time right here.
frames.art:
[1]---[3]
  /         \
[0]         [5]
  \         /
   [2]---[4]
[x] = visited, (x) = not yet

queue:  5            just popped: 4
node    0  1  2  3  4  5
level   0  1  1  2  2  3
        nothing new, level row unchanged

frames.label: Pop 5. Both of its neighbours are marked too, so nothing is pushed and the queue runs dry. The `while` loop ends here.
frames.art:
[1]---[3]
  /         \
[0]         [5]
  \         /
   [2]---[4]
[x] = visited, (x) = not yet

queue:  (empty)      just popped: 5
node    0  1  2  3  4  5
level   0  1  1  2  2  3
        nothing new, level row unchanged

frames.label: Every town was pushed once and popped once. Read the answer straight off the row: `level[5]` is 3, so town 5 is three roads away - and the same single run gave the distance to every other town at the same time.
frames.art:
[1]---[3]
  /         \
[0]         [5]
  \         /
   [2]---[4]
[x] = visited, (x) = not yet

queue:  (empty)      just popped: -
node    0  1  2  3  4  5
level   0  1  1  2  2  3
                       ^ the answer: 3 roads
